To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a missense mutation in the cytoskeletal protein ZASP leads to cytoskeletal and ion channel abnormalities in a mouse model of DCM.
the ZASP4 S196L mutation, which causes DCM in humans, also leads to cardiac conduction abnormalities in a mouse model, and that the S196L mutant protein interacts with ion channels.
a ZASP mutation leads to cardiac conduction defects, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death in a mouse model of cardiomyopathy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how mutations in the cytoskeleton of the heart can lead to arrhythmias.
the role of cytoskeletal proteins in the heart and the development of cardiomyopathies.
the molecular mechanisms that lead to cardiac conduction abnormalities and ventricular arrhythmias.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ZASP4 mutation leads to cytoskeletal and electrical abnormalities in a mouse model of DCM.
ZASP4 mutation leads to cardiac conduction defects, arrhythmias and cardiomyopathy in vivo, which is associated with altered cytoskeletal architecture and altered ion channel biology.

The main takeaway from our work is that

mutations in structural/cytoskeleton proteins can have a significant impact on the electrophysiology of cardiomyocytes and may contribute to the development of concomitant conduction system disease and arrhythmias.
mutations in cytoskeletal genes, such as Zasp, may cause cardiac dysfunction and arrhythmias through the modulation of ion channels.
a mutation in a protein that does not have a direct role in the ion channel biology, such as Zasp, can affect the function of ion channels and the cytoskeleton.
